newsitem.title: USA: Washington state Senate approves tax limit plan.
newsitem.headline: Washington state Senate approves tax limit plan.

text.p: The Washington state Senate on Wednesday approved a measure that caps the annual increase in state and local property tax collections at the rate of inflation.
The measure passed the Senate 33-16 after being approved earlier by the House. It now goes to Democratic Party Governor Gary Locke, who has not indicated whether he will sign it.
Legislative analysts calculated property tax collections in the state have increased at an average annual rate of 8.5 percent over the past 10 years.
"That's over two-and-a-half times the rate of growth of the average person's income," Republican Representative Mike Carrell said in the House debate on Monday. "It's not sustainable."
Carrell said Washington risked a property tax revolt if it did not takes steps to ease the growth in taxes.
County, city and fire district officials whose budgets rely on property taxes for the majority of their revenue initially opposed the legislature's property tax limit.
But when the measure was amended to allow local governments to exceed the inflation limit with a super-majority vote of 60 percent or more, their opposition subsided.

Thurston County Commission chairwoman Diane Oberquell told the Olympian newspaper that the county would lose $1 million in revenue annually if the tax increase was limited to inflation rather than six percent.
She said the county would be forced to cut services because the legislature continued to pass unfunded mandates on to counties.
Locke said he was worried the legislature was moving too fast in granting tax relief.
During his weekly news conference, he said he wanted to meet with legislative leaders to set priorities before deciding whether to sign the property tax cap.
The Senate measure, which would reduce taxes by an estimated $887 million over the next six years, is the second property tax reduction approved in the 1997 legislative session.
Last month Locke signed into law a 4.7 percent reduction in the state property tax that could be worth $379 million over the next six years if voters decide to make it permanent.
